title: Making capsule networks cope with hundreds of classes
paper_title: Using dynamic routing to extract intermediate features for developing scalable capsule networks
date_note: ICACCP 2019 (2nd Int. Conf. on Advanced Computational and Communication Paradigms), Gangtok, Sikkim, 25-28 Feb 2019 (from my knowledge of the venue; the PDF only shows the 2019 copyright line)
venue: 2nd International Conference on Advanced Computational and Communication Paradigms (ICACCP)
authors: B Mandal, Swarnendu Ghosh, R Sarkhel, N Das, M Nasipuri
summary: Capsule networks get slow and memory-hungry as the number of classes grows. We changed what their routing step produces, and trained faster on 199-class handwritten Bangla characters with higher accuracy.

body.p: Capsule networks are image classifiers that store each detected feature as a small list of numbers instead of a single value. They work nicely on ten-class problems such as digits, but they become slow and memory-hungry when the number of classes grows. We changed what the routing step of the network produces, so that its cost no longer depends on how many classes there are.

In an ordinary neural network, each unit outputs one number. A capsule outputs a vector, an arrow in a space of 8 or 16 dimensions. The length of the arrow says how likely it is that something is present, and its direction describes how it looks. A capsule network first builds many small primary capsules from convolutions. Then a step called dynamic routing lets these primary capsules vote for the final answer. The votes are weighed again and again during a single forward pass, and a vote counts more when it agrees with the combined answer.

In the original design the final layer holds one 16-dimensional capsule per class. That means the routing weights, and the memory they need, grow in direct proportion to the number of classes. Earlier work had also reported that capsule networks lose accuracy on more complicated data sets. Our own experience agreed: with many classes, there are many more possible agreements to check, and the network tends to overfit.

figure.alt: Diagram of the original capsule network: an image goes through a convolution, becomes primary capsules, is routed into one output capsule per class, and a decoder reconstructs the input.
figure.caption: The original design ends in one output capsule for every class, so the routing step grows with the number of classes.

body.p: We used dynamic routing for a different job. Instead of producing one capsule per class, the routing step produces a small set of feature capsules. Each of them is still a 16-dimensional vector, but it stands for a learned feature, not for a class. The feature capsules are flattened and passed to an ordinary fully connected layer, which turns them into class scores.

Think of describing a person by a few traits instead of keeping a separate checklist for everyone you might meet. The number of features can be much smaller than the number of classes, and the routing cost now depends only on the number of features. The decoder, which rebuilds the input image as a regulariser, also works from the full set of feature capsules, with no masking.

figure.alt: Diagram of the proposed network: the same primary capsules are routed into a few feature capsules, which are flattened into a fully connected layer for the classes, with a decoder for reconstruction.
figure.caption: In the proposed network the routing output is a small set of feature capsules, and a fully connected layer maps them to the classes.

body.p: We tested on five handwritten data sets from the Indic scripts: Bangla, Devanagari and Telugu numerals (10 classes each), Bangla basic characters (50 classes) and Bangla compound characters (199 classes). We compared against the standard capsule network on a GTX 1080 Ti with 11 GB of memory. The number of feature capsules, N<sub>features</sub>, was the main setting we varied.

On the ten-class numerals, accuracy stayed about the same. Training time per epoch (one pass over the training data) dropped, though. For Bangla numerals it went from 11.57 seconds with the standard network to 5.54 seconds with two feature capsules, and to 11.19 seconds with ten.
The gains show up on the larger problems:

ul: Bangla basic characters (50 classes): accuracy rose from 90.6% to 93.23% with eight feature capsules, and the epoch time fell from 120.61 to 25.74 seconds.
Bangla compound characters (199 classes): accuracy rose from 79.34% to 87.44% with six feature capsules, and the epoch time fell from 1,206.99 to 59.65 seconds.

body.callout: With six feature capsules on the 199-class compound characters, accuracy went from 79.34% to 87.44% while training time per epoch fell from 1,206.99 to 59.65 seconds.

body.p: Most of the saving comes from memory, not from faster arithmetic. Time per sample barely changed (0.0823 against 0.0662 seconds for the compound set with two feature capsules). But the standard network needed 2,057 MB per sample on that set, while ours needed between 667 and 801 MB whatever the number of classes. The largest possible batch size grew from 16 to as many as 1,520 images, which a GPU can process much more efficiently.

On the two larger sets, our best results also beat the other published methods we listed: 87.44% against 86.64% for the best earlier method on compound characters, and 93.23% against 92.15% on basic characters.

On the numerals, we saw no real accuracy gain, only the time saving. The speed advantage also disappears if N<sub>features</sub> is pushed up to the number of classes or beyond, so the feature count has to stay below the class count. We chose the number of feature capsules per data set, and we did not use a separate validation set: we kept the model with the best training performance and reported its test accuracy.

Because the decoder sees all feature capsules at once, the network can no longer produce a reconstruction of one specific class. We also did not study how feature capsules relate to equivariance, the property that motivated capsules in the first place. The paper lists both as open questions.

The practical point is that capsule networks no longer have to be limited to small label sets. A character set with a couple of hundred classes can now be trained in a minute per epoch on a single GPU, using the numbers above.
